summary: A notice from UCSB about changes to how network users log in to its On-line System. Since all network users shared one account, usage could not be tracked by site. From June 1, 1972, users supply their site name as the user name and their own name or NIC ID as the job name. A list of site designations is included.

plainLanguage.summary: UCSB changed how network users logged into its On-line System so it could identify the site using the service. The notice also clarifies that free access was for experimentation and casual use, while production work required a paid account.

subtitle: New login details for users of the UCSB On-line System

tldr.problem: All network users shared one UCSB account, making it difficult to track use by site.
tldr.mechanism: From June 1, users were to keep the listed user number and ID but enter their site designation as the user name and their own name or NIC ID as the job name.
tldr.outcome: The notice distinguishes experimental use from production use and explains when sites must open paid accounts.

today: RFC 350 is a notice about account use on the UCSB On-line System. It sets out a login change and distinguishes experimental access from production computing.

sections.title: Why the Login Procedure Changed
sections.content: UCSB had provided free use of its On-line System to network sites for about a year, with costs paid by the Computer Research Lab. All users had shared one account, so UCSB could not easily measure use by site. The notice reports 152 hours of connection time during April.
sections.plainLanguage: Users shared one account, so UCSB could not tell which site was using the system. The new login details were intended to identify the site.

sections.title: Login Details from June 1
sections.content: Starting June 1, 1972, network users were to enter User Number 196 and ID 57372 as before. They were to use their site's designation as the User Name and their own name, or NIC ID, as the Job Name. The notice includes a table matching connected organizations and hosts to their site designations.
sections.plainLanguage: Users kept the same user number and ID. They entered their site's name and their own name or NIC ID in the other login fields.

sections.title: Experimental and Production Use
sections.content:
UCSB says the free accounts were for network experimentation and casual use, including helping unfamiliar users learn about the system. Sites that planned to use it for production work were asked to open a private account and pay the computer charges.

Limited free remote batch support would continue for sites implementing or debugging network software. Production batch jobs also required a Computer Center account.
sections.plainLanguage: The free access was for trying the system and learning it. Sites using the computer for production work had to open a paid account.
